label: Long-term health
rationale: Health beyond today's symptoms: what's good for you, getting older, quitting smoking and allergies.
mixUps: karada ni ii keeps its ni even in casual talk. Getting older is toshi o toru, not furuku naru. tabako o yameru uses the same yameru as quitting a job (kaisha o yameru). An allergy is something you have: ebi no arerugii ga aru.

targets.trap: Not kore wa kenkou desu: kenkou describes a person's health, so food or habits that are good for you are karada ni ii (kenkou ni ii also works). Kenkouteki na shokuji (a healthy diet) and herushii (light, healthy food) are fine too.
targets.use: Said of food, drinks, sleep and habits: yasai wa karada ni ii. The opposite karada ni warui is just as common (tabako, yofukashi), and since ii conjugates from yoi, the softer negative is karada ni yokunai. Ni is kept even in casual speech.
targets.notes: Okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai (take care of yourself) is the stock sign-off with karada; casually, karada ni ki o tsukete ne.

example.romaji: yasai mo tabete. karada ni ii kara.
example.ja: 野菜も食べて。体にいいから。
example.english: Have some vegetables too. They're good for you.

examplePolite.romaji: yasai mo tabete kudasai. karada ni ii desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 野菜も食べてください。体にいいですから。
examplePolite.english: Please have some vegetables too. They're good for you.

targets.verbSense: take, get; with years, take them on
targets.trap: Not furuku naru, which is for things: people take on years, toshi o toru, and 'I'm getting old' is the past, toshi totta.
targets.use: Mostly said in the past for how you feel now: toshi totta naa (I'm getting old). The generic toshi o toru to... (as you get older...) is also common, and toshi totteru means someone is elderly. O often drops in casual talk (toshi totta) but is usually kept in toshi o toru to...
targets.notes: Keep apart from toshi ga ue (older than someone); otoshiyori is the polite word for the elderly. Mou toshi da kara (I'm not as young as I was) is the everyday shorthand you'll hear alongside toshi totta.

example.romaji: aa, toshi totta naa. sugu tsukareru.
example.ja: ああ、年取ったなあ。すぐ疲れる。
example.english: Man, I'm getting old. I get tired so fast.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi mo toshi o torimashita yo. sugu tsukarete shimau n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私も年を取りましたよ。すぐ疲れてしまうんです。
examplePolite.english: I've gotten old too. I get tired so easily now.

targets.verbSense: stop, give up (a habit, an activity); quitting a job is the same-sounding yameru (辞める), as in kaisha o yameru
targets.trap: English 'stop smoking' pulls toward tomeru, which is stopping a machine or a person (kuruma o tomeru). A habit you give up is yameru: tabako yameta.
targets.use: Heard as news, tabako yameta (I've quit), or advice, tabako yameta hou ga ii yo. Wa is common for contrast (tabako wa yameta), and osake o yameru works the same way.
targets.notes: Kin'en-chuu (I'm off cigarettes for now) is the other everyday phrase; kin'en on a sign means no smoking.

example.ja: タバコ、去年やめたんだ。

examplePolite.ja: タバコは去年やめました。
examplePolite.english: I gave up smoking last year.

targets.politeJa: アレルギーがあります
targets.verbSense: there is, exist (for things); here, have
targets.trap: Said the German way, arerugii (a-re-ru-gii), not like English 'allergy'. The cause goes in front: tamago arerugii, or tamago ni arerugii ga aru.
targets.use: Put the cause in front: tamago arerugii ga aru, or ebi no arerugii ga aru. Restaurants and clinics ask about it (arerugii wa arimasu ka?), and casual talk drops ga.
targets.notes: Hay fever is kafunshou (kafunshou nan desu), the allergy nearly everyone in Japan talks about each spring.

example.ja: エビアレルギーあるから、食べられない。
example.english: I'm allergic to shrimp, so I can't eat it.

examplePolite.romaji: ebi no arerugii ga aru node, taberaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: エビのアレルギーがあるので、食べられません。
examplePolite.english: I have a shrimp allergy, so I can't eat it.

reviewPool.english: sound comes out (of a TV, speaker, phone)
